docs.title: Cognibrain
docs.text:
Self-hosted engineering memory for coding agents.

Stop fixing the same agent mistake twice. Cognibrain stores durable engineering context — repo rules, reviewer corrections, failed commands, connector events, and patch evidence — then returns compact context before the next agent action.

  • Getting Started

    Install Cognibrain and have your first memory working in under 5 minutes.

    Quick Start

  • Guides

    Step-by-step walkthroughs for CLI, MCP, harness, connectors, and memory management.

    Explore Guides

  • Reference

    Complete API, SDK, CLI, and configuration reference documentation.

    API Reference

  • Operations

    Self-host, deploy with Docker, monitor health, and secure your instance.

    Operations Guide

docs.title: Commercial Operator UI Boundary
docs.text:
Status: superseded by ADR-0062.

Cognibrain keeps the CLI, API, SDK, connectors, harness templates, and docs in the MIT-licensed open-source package, but the browser Operator UI is a separately licensed commercial add-on. This prevents the paid control-plane experience from being accidentally redistributed through the OSS package while still letting licensed checkouts run the Next.js UI against the same local runtime.

docs.title: Repo-Owned Harness Package
docs.text:
Cognibrain will treat repository-owned harness files as the durable agent contract for memory use, while keeping user-level installation as a fallback. This prevents non-trivial agent work from depending on a user reminder or on a global Codex skill being selected.

The default config all flow writes native, commit-ready harness files into the repository for every supported harness. Codex keeps AGENTS.md as the always-on policy surface and adds .agents/skills/cognibrain/SKILL.md as the repo-local skill; other harnesses use their native discovery paths, not a hidden Cognibrain-only directory.

Repository contracts use portable commands such as npx @cognilabz/cognibrain instead of absolute local paths. The generated manifest remains the audit surface for paths, ownership mode, generation version, content hashes, ignored state, and check results.

Files that Cognibrain owns fully are managed; files that may contain project-local rules are advisory and updated only through marked Cognibrain blocks. Existing unmarked files are migrated by appending a marked block, never by blind overwrite. Install/update writes files and warnings, but does not stage, commit, prune, or edit project docs by default.

config all --check is an audit mode, not a default CI gate. It reports missing, stale, ignored, or non-portable contract files across all supported repo-owned harness contracts and exits successfully unless --strict is requested.

docs.title: Harness Judgment Checkpoints
docs.text: Cognibrain will allow the harness to pause an agent workflow at named Judgment Checkpoints, not only at coarse lifecycle calls such as context, guard, outcome, and patch evidence. This keeps semantic memory decisions close to the evidence that triggered them while preventing arbitrary interruption: every pause must be a typed Judgment Request with an expected verdict and fallback behavior.

docs.title: Memory Operating Protocol First
docs.text: Cognibrain v1 will ship the repo-installed Memory Operating Protocol as the primary artifact, with the CLI and runtime supporting that agent behavior rather than defining the product on their own. This keeps the market promise focused on agents that remember, judge, guard, store, and prove work through an installed harness/skill/plugin instead of asking users to assemble those behaviors manually from commands or APIs.

docs.title: Ledger-First Memory Model
docs.text: Cognibrain will treat the Memory Ledger as the source of truth and derive the Current Memory View from that ledger. This keeps every remembered claim explainable by its observations, corrections, judgments, outcomes, and evidence instead of relying on mutable memory rows whose origin and authority become unclear over time.

docs.title: Authority Levels on Ledger Events
docs.text: Cognibrain will attach an Authority Level to every Memory Ledger event so conflict handling is based on source precedence as well as judgment, relevance, and time. This prevents weaker observations or agent inferences from silently overriding stronger sources such as user corrections, maintainer-approved rules, repository documentation, or verified build and test evidence.

docs.title: Product-Defined Authority Ladder
docs.text: Cognibrain will ship a product-defined Authority Ladder for comparing Memory Ledger events, with repository-specific Authority Overrides allowed only as explicit exceptions. This gives the memory system useful conflict behavior out of the box while still allowing projects to encode unusual precedence rules, such as security policy outranking convenience requests or ADRs outranking general documentation.

docs.title: Low-Authority Memory as Candidate Evidence
docs.text: Cognibrain will treat low-authority or unresolved memories as Candidate Evidence for Judgment Requests rather than injecting them directly into agent context. This preserves useful signals from weak observations, stale outcomes, or agent inferences without letting them steer behavior until a higher-authority or harness-mediated judgment makes them safe to use.

docs.title: Explicit Promotion Into Current Memory View
docs.text: Cognibrain will require a Promotion Event before any candidate memory enters the Current Memory View. This prevents stored observations from becoming trusted recall merely because they exist: promotion must record the relevant Judgment Request, authority basis, confidence, and reason the memory is safe for agents to use.

docs.title: Explicit Retirement From Current Memory View
docs.text: Cognibrain will require a Retirement Event before a trusted memory leaves the Current Memory View. This keeps stale, superseded, contradicted, or unsafe memories from steering agents while preserving the Memory Ledger history that explains when the memory was trusted and why it stopped being trusted.

docs.title: Ephemeral Working Memory
docs.text: Cognibrain will distinguish Ephemeral Working Memory from durable Memory Ledger entries. This lets the harness support rich task-local reasoning, hypotheses, and in-progress notes without polluting durable memory; only information that passes a Judgment Request and Promotion Event should become durable trusted recall.

docs.title: Repo-Wide Shared Working Memory
docs.text:
Cognibrain will make Ephemeral Working Memory visible across capable agents in the same repository, not only agents participating in the same task. This supports the Mistake Prevention Claim: once Cognibrain observes an active mistake or task-local failure signal, other repo agents should be able to avoid repeating it even before the signal is promoted into durable memory.

Repo-wide sharing does not make working memory durable or trusted. Shared Working Memory remains outside the Memory Ledger unless a Judgment Request and Promotion Event make it safe to retain.

docs.title: Immediate Mistake Signals
docs.text:
Cognibrain will create a repo-wide Mistake Signal in Shared Working Memory as soon as it observes, is corrected about, or predicts an agent mistake. This supports the Mistake Prevention Claim by warning other capable agents immediately, while preserving the durable-memory boundary: a Mistake Signal still needs a Judgment Request and Promotion Event before it becomes trusted memory or an Action Guard.

Mistake Signals must distinguish confirmed and predicted cases. A Confirmed Mistake Signal comes from an observed failure or explicit correction; a Predicted Mistake Signal is a tentative pre-execution warning that should prevent likely repeat mistakes without pretending the failure has already happened.

docs.title: Predicted Signals Warn Before They Block
docs.text: Predicted Mistake Signals will warn by default and block only when they map to a high-authority Promoted Guard. This lets Cognibrain prevent likely repeat mistakes without freezing agent progress on prediction alone, while still allowing hard stops for risks backed by promoted user corrections, safety rules, or verified failures.

docs.title: Record Mistake Signal Outcomes
docs.text: Cognibrain will require agents to record how they handled Mistake Signals. Blocking signals and Promoted Guard matches require an explicit outcome such as changed course, appealed, or judged irrelevant; ordinary warnings require a lightweight outcome such as followed, ignored, or seen.

docs.title: Mistake Prevention Over Feature Parity
docs.text: Cognibrain will use the Mistake Prevention Claim as its Market Leadership Standard instead of copying the feature lists of existing memory tools. The product should be judged by whether capable agents stop repeating known mistakes in real work, with other surfaces and features treated as support for that outcome.

docs.title: Forget, Retire, and Erase
docs.text: Cognibrain will treat Forget as the user-facing request to stop using a memory, implemented by a Retirement Event by default. Erase is reserved for destructive privacy, security, or legal deletion. This preserves auditability for ordinary memory maintenance while keeping a clear path for cases where retaining ledger history would be unsafe or impermissible.

docs.title: Brain Lifecycle
docs.text: Cognibrain will use the Brain Lifecycle as its top-level product model: notice, remember, warn, reflect, dream, improve, and forget. The metaphor is user-facing, but every verb must map to strict system behavior so the product remains operationally testable against the Mistake Prevention Claim.

docs.title: Notice Before Memory
docs.text: Cognibrain will treat Notice as the first-class lifecycle trigger for possible memory-worthy events such as mistakes, corrections, contradictions, repeated failures, repository rules, risky actions, and preferences. Notice may create Candidate Evidence or a Mistake Signal, but it must not create durable trusted memory without the later judgment and promotion steps.

docs.title: Save Is Not Remember
docs.text: Cognibrain will distinguish Save from Remember. Save captures raw material into Shared Working Memory or the Memory Ledger without making it trusted recall; Remember requires judgment, authority, and a Promotion Event before information can enter the Current Memory View and steer future agents.

docs.title: Explainable Warn Lifecycle
docs.text: Cognibrain will treat Warn as the lifecycle step that delivers Mistake Signals and Action Guards before an agent acts. Warn can produce soft warnings or hard blocks, but every delivery must be explainable through signal type, authority, evidence, and the Signal Outcome the agent records.

docs.title: Immediate Reflect Lifecycle
docs.text: Cognibrain will run Reflect after every meaningful task outcome rather than waiting only for background Dream Cycles. Reflect reviews what happened, which signals or guards were followed or ignored, what mistakes were avoided or repeated, and what should become Candidate Evidence, a Mistake Signal, or a later Judgment Request.

docs.title: Dream Proposes Before It Applies
docs.text: Cognibrain will allow Dream Cycles to propose promotions, retirements, guard improvements, contradiction resolutions, and summaries automatically. Dream must not apply trusted memory changes unless a Judgment Request approves the change or an operator-approved rule explicitly allows that class of change.

docs.title: Improve Changes Future Behavior
docs.text: Cognibrain will treat Improve as a change to future agent behavior, not merely the storage of a better memory. An improvement may strengthen a guard, improve a Notice trigger, clarify an authority rule, retire noisy memory, promote a correction, or add a benchmark case; if future behavior does not change, Cognibrain has not improved.

docs.title: Harness Trigger Contract
docs.text: Cognibrain will require every supported Harness to implement the same Harness Trigger Contract, even when adapters differ for Codex, Copilot, Claude, Hermes, or other agents. A harness is supported only when Harness Conformance proves it triggers the Brain Lifecycle at required workflow moments, including session start, before action, after tool result, after user correction, before final answer, after task outcome, and session end.

docs.title: Fixed Harness Trigger Points
docs.text: Cognibrain will define a fixed minimum set of Harness Trigger Points for every supported harness: session_start, before_action, after_tool_result, after_user_correction, before_final_answer, after_task_outcome, and session_end. Each adapter may map those events to its host agent differently, but Harness Conformance must prove the semantic trigger is present and handled.

docs.title: Trace-Backed Harness Conformance
docs.text: Cognibrain will require Harness Conformance to use Harness Traces captured from real adapter execution, not fake transcripts alone. Fake transcripts may test parsers, schemas, and lower-level contract logic, but a harness is certified only when a real trace proves trigger ordering, causality, delivered Cognibrain responses, recorded outcomes, and failure handling.

docs.title: Harness Mutation Tests
docs.text: Certified harnesses must include Harness Mutation Tests that disable or corrupt required Harness Trigger Points and cause Harness Conformance to fail. A Harness Trace proves the happy path ran; mutation proves the conformance suite can detect broken lifecycle triggering instead of merely accepting a plausible transcript.

docs.title: Certified vs Best-Effort Harnesses
docs.text: Cognibrain will distinguish Certified Harnesses from Best-Effort Harnesses. A Certified Harness requires trace-backed, mutation-tested Harness Conformance; unsupported or untraceable adapters may still operate as Best-Effort Harnesses, but they cannot claim the full Brain Lifecycle or Mistake Prevention Claim. This protects the market promise without blocking experimental or partially capable integrations.

docs.title: One-Time Harness Certification
docs.text: Cognibrain treats Certified Harness status as persistent after the first successful Harness Conformance run. Certification does not automatically expire, demote to Best-Effort Harness, or enter a review-required state when the harness package, Harness Trigger Contract, or host workflow changes. This favors stable product language and low integration friction over freshness-scoped certification; any future freshness signal must be named separately from Certified Harness.

docs.title: Certification Evidence Is Historical
docs.text: Certified Harnesses will expose Certification Evidence: the original Harness Trace and Harness Mutation Test record that earned certification. This evidence makes the claim auditable, but it is not a freshness proof, expiry marker, or trigger for automatic recertification. The decision preserves one-time Harness Certification while still making the basis of the claim inspectable.

docs.title: Unavailable Trigger Points Force Best-Effort
docs.text: If a host tool cannot expose a required Harness Trigger Point, its adapter must be treated as a Best-Effort Harness even when every available trigger works correctly. Partial lifecycle coverage is useful, but it cannot honestly support the full Brain Lifecycle or Mistake Prevention Claim.

docs.title: Best-Effort Signals
docs.text: Best-Effort Harnesses may still run Action Guards and warnings, but every emitted signal must clearly carry best-effort status. This keeps partial mistake protection available when a host cannot support the full Harness Trigger Contract, while preventing those signals from being mistaken for the full Mistake Prevention Claim.

docs.title: Best-Effort Signals Are Warning-Only
docs.text: Best-Effort Signals may warn but must not block. Blocking is reserved for a Certified Harness applying a high-authority Promoted Guard, because partial lifecycle coverage can advise an agent but cannot justify stopping it under the full Mistake Prevention Claim.

docs.title: All Signals Record Outcomes
docs.text: Agents must record a Signal Outcome for every delivered signal, including Best-Effort Signals. Blocking and certified signals require explicit outcomes such as changed course, appealed, or judged irrelevant; Best-Effort Signals may use lightweight outcomes such as seen, followed, or ignored. This preserves the Reflect and Dream feedback loop without turning partial warnings into heavy protocol work.

docs.title: Signal Noise Evidence Feeds Dream
docs.text: Repeated ignored or judged irrelevant Signal Outcomes become Signal Noise Evidence for Dream to consider retiring, weakening, or rewriting noisy warnings. This lets Cognibrain learn from annoying or stale signals without letting a few dismissed warnings automatically delete useful protection.

docs.title: Signal Noise Threshold
docs.text: Dream needs a Signal Noise Threshold before proposing that a warning be retired, weakened, or rewritten. The default threshold is at least three ignored or judged irrelevant Signal Outcomes spanning at least two agents or sessions. One dismissal is noise; repeated dismissal across context is evidence.

docs.title: Single Developer Scope
docs.text:
Status: superseded by ADR-0061.

Cognibrain is scoped to a single developer, not teams, workspaces, organizations, or tenants. Memory, harness behavior, Signal Noise Thresholds, and operator surfaces should be designed around one developer managing repo-scoped memory across their own capable agents. This keeps the product focused on preventing one developer's agents from repeating known mistakes instead of drifting into collaboration and account-management features.

docs.title: Solo-Dev Only Docs
docs.text:
Status: superseded by ADR-0061.

Cognibrain docs will present solo-dev as the product setup path and benchmark only as a proof lab. Team, workspace, organization, tenant, and enterprise profiles are outside the single-developer memory solution and should not appear as product scope in setup, reference, operations, or connector documentation.

docs.title: Repo-Local Signal Noise Threshold
docs.text: The Signal Noise Threshold is a repo-local single-developer Operator setting. The default remains at least three ignored or judged irrelevant Signal Outcomes spanning at least two agents or sessions; the Operator may override that threshold per repo only with an explicit reason. This keeps Dream tunable for one developer's repo without turning warning weakening into an invisible global behavior.

docs.title: Bidirectional Signal Noise Threshold Overrides
docs.text: Signal Noise Threshold Overrides may raise or lower the repo-local threshold. Raising the threshold requires more evidence before Dream proposes weakening a warning; lowering the threshold makes warning weakening easier and must be visibly marked that way, with the Operator's explicit reason. Both directions remain repo-local and only affect Dream proposals, not automatic memory changes.

docs.title: Lowered Thresholds Default to Best-Effort
docs.text: A lowered Signal Noise Threshold Override applies only to Best-Effort Signals by default. Applying a lowered threshold to Certified Harness warnings requires a separate Certified Warning Noise Override with the Operator's explicit reason, because it makes trusted protection easier to weaken. Raising the threshold may apply broadly because it requires more evidence before Dream proposes warning changes.

docs.title: Certified Warning Noise Overrides Persist
docs.text: A Certified Warning Noise Override persists until the Operator retires it, instead of requiring re-confirmation every time Dream uses it. The trade-off is intentional: persistent overrides keep solo-dev operation usable, while mandatory visible attribution on every affected Dream proposal preserves trust around Certified Harness warnings and keeps weakening trusted protection from becoming hidden or automatic.

docs.title: Signal Appeals Are Evidence Only
docs.text: When an agent appeals a warning or block, Cognibrain records the appeal as Candidate Evidence for Dream instead of immediately weakening the signal or guard. This keeps correction pressure visible without letting one objection silently erode protection; warnings may still be ignored with a Signal Outcome, while blocks require explicit Operator override.

docs.title: Block Overrides Are One-Time by Default
docs.text: Operator Block Overrides are one-time by default. Persistent bypasses require a separate explicit Operator decision with a reason, because a single unblock should let the current action proceed without quietly becoming a durable policy change that weakens future protection.

docs.title: Block Overrides Require Reasons
docs.text: Every Operator Block Override requires a short reason, including one-time overrides. This adds a small amount of friction at the moment protection is bypassed, but it gives Dream usable evidence about whether a block was wrong, too broad, or intentionally overridden for a specific case.

docs.title: Override Reasons Are Private by Default
docs.text: Override Reasons are private local evidence by default. Cognibrain may later surface only a sanitized summary to agents when that helps explain a decision or guide future behavior, because raw override text can contain secrets, frustration, half-formed judgment, or project details that should not be injected into agent context.

docs.title: Sanitized Summaries Use Harness Judgment
docs.text: Sanitized Summaries of Override Reasons are created through Harness-Mediated Judgment, not deterministic redaction alone. Deterministic redaction may pre-filter obvious secrets, but deciding what is safe and useful to surface is semantic judgment and must go through the harness so raw private evidence is not accidentally injected into agent context.

docs.title: Approved Sanitized Summaries Are Stored
docs.text: Approved Sanitized Summaries are stored durably once created and linked back to the private Override Reason or evidence that produced them. This keeps agent-facing explanations stable, auditable, and reproducible without repeatedly re-judging raw private evidence or letting future summaries drift.

docs.title: Sanitized Summaries Can Be Approved Automatically
docs.text: Sanitized Summaries may be approved automatically by the Harness-Mediated Judgment that creates them, without a separate Operator approval step. This favors low-friction agent guidance while accepting the privacy risk of automated approval; the durable summary must still be linked back to the private evidence so the Operator can audit, retire, or correct it later.

docs.title: Sanitized Summaries Are Silent Unless Exceptional
docs.text: Automatically approved Sanitized Summaries are stored and usable without appearing in a routine Operator review queue. They surface to the Operator only through a Summary Exception, such as a correction, appeal, audit request, or suspected privacy or safety problem; this keeps the low-friction path chosen for automatic approval while preserving a way to inspect and repair bad summaries.

docs.title: Contested Summaries Remain Usable
docs.text: When a Summary Exception is triggered, the Sanitized Summary is marked as a Contested Summary but remains usable by default. This avoids disrupting low-friction agent guidance while making the risk visible; a later review, judgment, correction, or retirement event can still change or stop use of the summary.

docs.title: Contested Summaries Carry Agent-Visible Markers
docs.text: When a Contested Summary is delivered to an agent, Cognibrain shows a concise Contested Marker. The marker tells the agent to treat the summary carefully while keeping the private reason, reason category, and underlying evidence hidden; this preserves agent caution without leaking the Summary Exception context.

docs.title: Contested Markers Mean Caution, Not Prohibition
docs.text: Agents treat a Contested Marker as caution, not prohibition. They may use the Contested Summary when helpful, but should not rely on it as the sole basis for risky actions or strong claims; this preserves usability while preventing contested guidance from carrying normal-trust authority.

docs.title: Contested Risk Is Judged Through the Harness
docs.text: Whether a Contested Use would make a Contested Summary the sole basis for a risky action or strong claim is decided case-by-case through Harness-Mediated Judgment. Deterministic examples may guide the judgment, but they are not the final authority, because risk and claim strength are semantic decisions that depend on the action, context, and reliance pattern.

docs.title: Unavailable Contested Risk Judgment Requires Independent Support
docs.text: If Contested Risk Judgment is unavailable, agents degrade to caution instead of blocking or treating the Contested Summary as normal context. The agent may continue with risky actions or strong claims only when Independent Support exists, so contested guidance stays usable without becoming the sole authority when the harness cannot judge the risk.

docs.title: Independent Support Is Semantic
docs.text: Independent Support may be any non-contested, task-relevant evidence judged sufficient by the agent or harness, such as current file inspection, tests, operator input, or non-contested memory. This keeps the fallback usable in real work while rejecting weak substitutes like a stale, irrelevant, or merely second memory item.

docs.title: Independent Support Use Records Outcomes
docs.text: When an agent uses Independent Support while acting on a Contested Summary, Cognibrain records a lightweight Independent Support Outcome. This keeps contested-summary behavior auditable without turning every use into a heavy review flow, and prevents strong claims or risky actions from disappearing from the evidence trail.

docs.title: Independent Support Outcomes Store Compact Fields
docs.text: Independent Support Outcomes store the Contested Summary identifier, support type, confidence, and brief rationale. This is enough for audit and Dream to understand why contested guidance was usable, while avoiding full evidence snapshots that would add noise or risk leaking private or task-local details.

docs.title: Trust-First Memory
docs.text: Cognibrain defaults to Trust-First Memory: protecting the Mistake Prevention Claim matters more than minimizing every interruption. The product may add friction when that friction helps stop agents from repeating known mistakes, because the market promise is trustable memory rather than silent context stuffing.

docs.title: Avoid Multi-Developer Positioning Until Sync Exists
docs.text: Cognibrain memory is carried by the repository, so memory files can move with a checkout and may be inherited by another developer. That technical portability should not be positioned as collaborative memory until Cognibrain has distributed sync and conflict handling, because normal version-control merges can create divergent memory histories.

docs.title: Harness-Native Operator Experience For The Greenfield Rebuild
docs.text: The greenfield memory solution has no Operator UI or commercial dashboard product surface. This is not an instruction to delete the existing solution's legacy dashboard code or historical docs; it only means the rebuilt solution should not include that surface. Operator-facing work belongs in harness-native prompts, Action Guards, and the text-first CLI, because the memory product must act at the moment agents work instead of requiring a separate dashboard habit.

docs.title: Core Market Promise
docs.text: The greenfield memory solution uses "repo brain for agentic development" as the narrative wrapper, but its hard market promise is narrower and measurable: capable agents should stop repeating corrected mistakes. This rejects broad "remember everything" or personal memory OS positioning for V1 because those claims are easier to fake and harder to prove.

docs.title: Product Mistakes Are Corrected Bad-Work Risks
docs.text: For the greenfield memory solution, a mistake means a corrected repeated or repeatable agent failure that caused, or would likely cause, bad work if repeated. This excludes generic annoyance, merely suboptimal choices, and test/build failures as the only category, keeping the Mistake Prevention Claim strong enough to prove without narrowing it to compiler output.

docs.title: Recurrence Prevention Before Noise Reduction
docs.text: When the greenfield solution identifies a Product Mistake, it optimizes first for preventing recurrence and only then for reducing warning noise. This preserves trust in the Mistake Prevention Claim; interruption reduction remains important, but it cannot come before stopping corrected bad-work risks from repeating.

docs.title: Product Mistake Evidence Bar
docs.text: The greenfield solution may create or strengthen a Product Mistake from an explicit developer correction, failed verification tied to an agent action, or repeated agent failure with clear evidence. It should not treat any failed command, ordinary exploration failure, or agent self-reflection alone as enough evidence, because that would turn mistake prevention into noisy generic logging.

docs.title: Full-Spectrum Mistake Surface
docs.text: The greenfield solution should allow Product Mistakes across the full development surface: style, preferences, architecture, commands, safety, docs, and developer-state signals. This broad category scope does not lower the Product Mistake or Product Mistake Evidence bars; it prevents V1 from being merely a command/test failure memory while avoiding the trap where every annoyance or mood signal becomes a mistake.

docs.title: Mistake Replay Proof for V1 Claim
docs.text: Cognibrain V1 will prove its Mistake Prevention Claim through Mistake Replay Proof: real corrected Product Mistakes are replayed through a Certified Harness, and the product must show the agent avoids repeating them. This rejects a benchmark leaderboard, broad brain-behavior demo, or single-harness-only showcase as the primary V1 proof because those can look impressive while failing to prove the market promise directly.

docs.title: Integration Layer
docs.text:
The integration layer adapts different client protocols to the unified HTTP API:

Component Protocol Consumers MCP Server stdio (Model Context Protocol) Codex, Cursor, MCP-native agents Harness CLI Shell process + JSON stdout Any shell-capable agent, git hooks, CI SDK/HTTP REST over HTTP Product integrations and custom runtimes

All three surfaces are stateless proxies — they translate requests into API calls and format responses for their protocol.

docs.title: Memory Engine
docs.text:
The core memory engine handles:

  • Storage: CRUD operations on memory items
  • Retrieval: Relevance-ranked context retrieval within token budgets
  • Graph: Relationships between memories (supersedes, contradicts, relates-to)
  • Policy: Scoping rules, access control, and governance
  • Guards: Pre-action safety checks against stored knowledge

docs.title: Storage Layer
docs.text:
Pluggable storage backends:

Backend Use Case Characteristics Local JSON Solo development Zero-config, file-based, fast startup SQLite Local durable Single-file database, good for single-machine PostgreSQL Team/production Full ACID, concurrent access, scalable

docs.title: Dream Cycle Engine
docs.text:
Runs asynchronously to maintain memory health:

  • Staleness detection
  • Contradiction identification
  • Summary consolidation
  • Harness and CLI review queue management

docs.title: Connector System
docs.text:
Bidirectional integration with external systems:

  • Ingest: Pull events from external systems → create memories
  • Emit: Push memory-linked context back to external systems
  • Sync: Bidirectional state synchronization

docs.title: Agent Lifecycle Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant API as HTTP API
    participant Engine as Memory Engine
    participant Store as Storage

    Agent->>API: POST /api/context
    API->>Engine: getContextPack(task, budget)
    Engine->>Store: query relevant memories
    Store-->>Engine: ranked memories
    Engine-->>API: context pack
    API-->>Agent: {context, memoriesUsed, tokenCount}

    Agent->>API: POST /api/guard
    API->>Engine: checkGuard(action)
    Engine->>Store: query guards & blockers
    Store-->>Engine: matching guards
    Engine-->>API: guard result
    API-->>Agent: {allowed, warnings, blockers}

    Agent->>API: POST /api/outcome
    API->>Engine: recordOutcome(command, exitCode)
    Engine->>Store: persist outcome
    API-->>Agent: {recorded: true}

docs.title: Connector Ingest Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Ext as External System
    participant Conn as Connector Driver
    participant API as HTTP API
    participant Engine as Memory Engine

    Ext->>Conn: Event (webhook/poll)
    Conn->>Conn: Normalize to memory fields
    Conn->>API: POST /api/memories
    API->>Engine: store(normalizedMemory)
    Engine-->>API: {id, stored: true}

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. Local-first: Works fully offline on a single machine with no external dependencies
  2. Text-first: CLI output is readable in small terminals, CI logs, and remote shells
  3. Daemon-optional: Direct local access available for simple setups; daemon for production
  4. Surface-agnostic: Same memory engine regardless of how you connect
  5. Evidence-backed: Claims and benchmarks require artifact proof
  6. Operator-in-the-loop: Automated maintenance surfaces items for human review, never auto-deletes

docs.title: Domain Glossary
docs.text: Precise definitions for Cognibrain's domain language. Using consistent terminology prevents confusion between concepts — especially when communicating with coding agents.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
A durable, scoped fact, correction, procedure, preference, or evidence item that can be recalled before an agent or operator acts.

Avoid

Don't use "note", "snippet", or "random context" when referring to memories. A memory is structured, scoped, and participates in retrieval ranking.

docs.title: Operator
docs.text:
The human or service account responsible for inspecting, correcting, approving, and maintaining Cognibrain memory state.

Avoid

Don't use "admin" when the role is about memory stewardship rather than deployment.

docs.title: Operator Experience
docs.text:
The V1 workflow where the developer inspects, corrects, approves, and maintains Cognibrain memory through harness prompts, action guards, and CLI commands in the same work context.

Avoid

Don't use "Operator UI", "dashboard", or "browser control plane" for the V1 product surface.

docs.title: Operator CLI
docs.text:
The text-first command surface for setup, status, memory work, connectors, proof, and automation.

Avoid

Don't use "TUI" or "dashboard" when referring to the CLI.

docs.title: Connector
docs.text:
A configured integration source or sink that can ingest external events, surface review queues, or write back memory-linked context.

Avoid

Don't use "plugin" when the component syncs external operational data.

docs.title: Harness
docs.text:
An installable agent or shell lifecycle integration that asks Cognibrain for context, guards actions, and records outcomes.

Avoid

Don't use "connector" when the component wraps an agent workflow.

docs.title: Dream Cycle
docs.text:
A memory maintenance pass that can detect stale or contradictory memories, produce summaries, and schedule operator review.

Avoid

Don't use "cleanup job" or "cron" when discussing the domain behavior.

docs.title: Context Pack
docs.text: A curated, token-budgeted collection of memories relevant to a specific task. Returned by the context command and MCP tool.

docs.title: Action Guard
docs.text:
A pre-action check that evaluates a planned operation against stored knowledge. Can result in:

  • Allowed — no known issues
  • Warned — proceed with caution
  • Blocked — operation should not proceed

docs.title: Patch Evidence
docs.text: A record of what happened during a task: files changed, commands executed, and memories that were recalled or created.

docs.title: Correction
docs.text: A human-provided fix or clarification stored as a high-authority memory. Corrections take precedence over auto-ingested facts.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: A recorded result of a command execution, including exit code and optional stderr. Used to build history and improve future guards.

docs.title: Staleness
docs.text: A memory's state when it hasn't been recalled or referenced for an extended period. Stale memories are candidates for operator review.

docs.title: Contradiction
docs.text: A detected conflict between two or more memories that make opposing claims. Surfaced for operator resolution.

docs.title: Consolidation
docs.text: The process of merging related, overlapping memories into a single cleaner memory. Always requires operator approval.

docs.title: Surface
docs.text: An integration protocol through which agents or operators interact with Cognibrain (CLI, MCP, HTTP API, SDK).

docs.title: Daemon
docs.text: The local HTTP API server process that serves all surfaces. Optional for simple local-direct usage; required for production.

docs.title: Profile
docs.text: A pre-configured set of defaults for the single-developer workflow or benchmark proof lab (solo-dev, benchmark).

docs.title: Runtime Root
docs.text: The directory where Cognibrain stores runtime state (config, memories, connector state, logs). Default: .cognibrain/.

docs.title: Scope Hierarchy
docs.text: Scope Visibility Example global All contexts "Always use semantic versioning" repo Within a specific repository "This project uses Jest for testing" user For a specific user, any repo "I prefer verbose error messages" task Relevant to task types "Release tasks require changelog updates"

docs.title: Storage & Persistence
docs.text:
Cognibrain supports multiple storage backends, from zero-config local files to production-grade PostgreSQL.

For production-style deployments, Cognibrain uses DB-primary MemoryRepository paths for SQLite and Postgres. Runtime writes go to the target database through row-backed repository operations; local JSON snapshots are backup, migration, or solo-dev artifacts rather than the primary write path.

docs.title: Local JSON
docs.text:
The default for solo-dev profile. Zero configuration required.

npx cognibrain init --yes  # Uses local-json by default
  • Location: .cognibrain/memories.json
  • Best for: Solo developers, quick experiments, local agent memory
  • Limitations: Single process only, no concurrent writes, not suitable for remote daemon sharing

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
Local durable storage in a single file.

npx cognibrain connections add storage-sqlite
  • Location: .cognibrain/cognibrain.db
  • Best for: Single-machine deployments needing durability and query capabilities
  • Limitations: Single-writer at a time, not suitable for multi-node

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Full relational database for production-style or high-volume single-developer deployments.

npx cognibrain connections add storage-postgres --url-env MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL
  • Connection: Via MEMORY_DB_URL or MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL
  • Best for: Larger single-developer stores, production-style daemon deployments, external backup workflows
  • Features: Full ACID, concurrent access, backup/restore, replication

docs.title: Memory Item
docs.text:
Every memory stored in Cognibrain has this structure:

Field Type Description id string Unique identifier (e.g., mem_abc123) content string The memory text scope enum repo, user, global, task status enum active, stale, review, archived source string How this memory was created authority number Ranking weight (corrections > auto-ingested) createdAt timestamp Creation time updatedAt timestamp Last modification lastRecalledAt timestamp Last time included in a context pack recallCount number Total times recalled metadata object Additional structured data

docs.title: Memory Relationships
docs.text:
Memories can have directed relationships:

graph LR
    A[Memory A] -->|supersedes| B[Memory B]
    A -->|contradicts| C[Memory C]
    D[Memory D] -->|relates-to| A
Relationship Meaning supersedes This memory replaces an older one contradicts These memories conflict (needs resolution) relates-to These memories are topically related

docs.title: Evidence Record
docs.text:
Patch evidence is stored alongside memories:

Field Type Description evidenceId string Unique identifier task string Task description files string[] Files changed commands string[] Commands executed memoriesUsed string[] Memory IDs that were recalled createdAt timestamp When the evidence was recorded

docs.title: Retrieval & Ranking
docs.text:
When a context pack is requested, the retrieval engine:

  1. Filters by scope (repo, user, global) and status (active only)
  2. Scores relevance against the task description
  3. Ranks by composite score: relevance × authority × freshness
  4. Fills the token budget with highest-ranked items
  5. Formats into a compact context string
graph LR
    A[All Active Memories] --> B[Scope Filter]
    B --> C[Relevance Scoring]
    C --> D[Authority Weighting]
    D --> E[Token Budget Fill]
    E --> F[Context Pack]

docs.title: Scoring Factors
docs.text: Factor Weight Description Relevance High Semantic similarity to task description Authority Medium Source credibility (operator > agent > auto) Freshness Low Recency of creation or last recall Recall frequency Low How often this memory has been useful

docs.title: Local → SQLite
docs.text:
npx cognibrain connections add storage-sqlite
npx cognibrain service restart

docs.title: SQLite → PostgreSQL
docs.text:
export MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL="postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/cognibrain"
npx cognibrain connections add storage-postgres --url-env MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL
npx cognibrain service restart

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
# Local JSON — just copy the file
cp .cognibrain/memories.json backup/

# SQLite
sqlite3 .cognibrain/cognibrain.db ".backup backup/cognibrain.db"

# PostgreSQL
pg_dump $MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL > backup/cognibrain.sql

docs.title: Storage Verification
docs.text:
Verify storage health for your deployment:

npx cognibrain doctor --fix
npx cognibrain connections doctor

For PostgreSQL specifically:

npm run internal -- verify:postgres

docs.title: Architecture Decisions
docs.text: Cognibrain records significant architectural decisions as ADRs (Architecture Decision Records). Each ADR captures the context, decision, and consequences of a choice that affects the system's structure.

docs.title: ADR-0001: Commercial Operator UI Boundary
docs.text:
Status: Superseded by ADR-0062

Context: Cognibrain previously had both an open-source runtime and a commercial operator experience. The boundary between what's MIT-licensed and what's commercially licensed needed to be clear and enforceable.

Decision: Superseded. V1 no longer includes an Operator UI as a product surface; operator work is harness-native and CLI-backed.

Consequences:

  • The previous commercial dashboard boundary is no longer current product scope
  • Future browser inspection tools require a new ADR before becoming product surface

docs.title: ADR-0002: Repo-Owned Harness Package
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Context: Agent memory use should not depend on a user reminder or on a global Codex skill being selected. Harness instructions need to live where each agent host can discover them from the repository.

Decision: config all writes native, commit-ready repository harness files for every supported harness. Codex uses AGENTS.md plus .agents/skills/cognibrain/SKILL.md; other harnesses use their native discovery paths. Global installation remains a fallback.

Consequences:

  • Repository contracts use portable commands such as npx @cognilabz/cognibrain
  • Managed files can be fully regenerated; advisory files are updated only through marked Cognibrain blocks
  • .cognibrain-harness-package.json remains the audit surface for paths, hashes, ownership mode, ignored state, and check results
  • config all --check reports drift across all supported repo-owned harness contracts by default without acting as a hard CI gate

docs.title: Writing New ADRs
docs.text: When making a significant architectural decision, create a new ADR:

docs.title: When to Write an ADR
docs.text:
• A decision affects the public API surface
  • A decision changes the storage model or data flow
  • A decision sets a boundary between OSS and commercial
  • A decision constrains future implementation choices
  • Multiple reasonable alternatives were considered

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
# [Title]

[Brief description of the decision and its rationale]

ADRs are stored in docs/adr/ and kept deliberately concise. They record the what and why, not the how (that's in the code).

docs.title: File Naming
docs.text:
docs/adr/NNNN-short-title.md

Sequential numbering, lowercase with hyphens.

docs.title: Principles Behind Decisions
docs.text:
The following principles guide architectural decisions:

  1. Local-first — everything works on a single machine without network
  2. Text-first — CLI output is the primary interface, not a GUI
  3. Evidence-backed — claims require artifact proof
  4. Surface-agnostic — the memory engine doesn't know which surface is calling it
  5. Operator-in-the-loop — automated processes surface items for human review
  6. Harness-native operator experience — agent-facing work happens in harnesses; explicit inspection and repair happens through the CLI

docs.title: Connector SDK
docs.text: Build community connectors that integrate external systems with Cognibrain's memory engine.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A connector is a configured integration that can:

  • Ingest events from external systems → create memories
  • Emit memory-linked context back to external systems
  • Sync bidirectional state between systems

docs.title: Scaffold a Connector
docs.text:
Use the CLI to generate the boilerplate:

npx cognibrain sdk platform acme-tracker \
  --kind issue_tracker \
  --direction ingest \
  --auth token \
  --out integrations/acme-tracker

This generates:

integrations/acme-tracker/
├── manifest.json         # Connector metadata
├── adapter.ts           # TypeScript adapter entrypoint
├── .env.example         # Required environment variables
├── fixtures/            # Test fixtures
│   └── sample-event.json
├── tests/
│   └── adapter.test.ts  # Smoke test
└── README.md            # Connector documentation

docs.title: Connector Kinds
docs.text: Kind Examples issue_tracker Jira, Linear, Asana, ClickUp, GitHub Issues code_host GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps chat Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams docs Confluence, Notion, Google Drive calendar Google Calendar observability Sentry, Datadog, PagerDuty, PostHog email Gmail storage PostgreSQL (as connector)

docs.title: TypeScript Adapter
docs.text:
import { createPlatformIntegration } from "@cognilabz/cognibrain/sdk/typescript/connectors";

export const acmeTracker = createPlatformIntegration({
  id: "acme-tracker",
  kind: "issue_tracker",
  direction: "ingest",
  version: "1.0.0",

  auth: {
    method: "token",
    envVar: "ACME_API_TOKEN",
    scopes: ["read:issues", "read:comments"],
  },

  rateLimits: {
    requestsPerMinute: 30,
  },

  handlers: {
    async fetchEvents(config) {
      const response = await fetch(`${config.baseUrl}/api/issues`, {
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${config.token}` },
      });
      const issues = await response.json();

      return issues.map(issue => ({
        externalId: issue.id,
        type: "issue_update",
        content: `[${issue.key}] ${issue.title}: ${issue.status}`,
        timestamp: issue.updatedAt,
        metadata: {
          issueKey: issue.key,
          status: issue.status,
          assignee: issue.assignee,
        },
      }));
    },

    async testConnection(config) {
      const response = await fetch(`${config.baseUrl}/api/me`, {
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${config.token}` },
      });
      return { success: response.ok };
    },
  },
});

docs.title: Quality Guidelines
docs.text: A good community connector should:

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Map external records to durable memory fields
  • Keep secrets in environment variables (never in code or config files)
  • Include a small fixture and smoke test
  • Provide a testConnection handler for health checks
  • Document rate limits and required scopes

docs.title: Recommended
docs.text:
• Provide a dry-run or preview path
  • Handle pagination for large data sets
  • Implement incremental sync (only fetch new events)
  • Include retry logic with exponential backoff
  • Log structured output for debugging

  3. Do not weaken benchmark gates to make a change pass
  4. Keep docs readable for non-developers when behavior changes user expectations
  5. Do not store secrets or real sensitive transcripts in fixtures, docs, screenshots, or examples

docs.title: Unit Tests
docs.text:
Use Vitest for all unit and integration tests:

import { describe, it, expect, beforeEach } from "vitest";

describe("MemoryEngine", () => {
  let engine: MemoryEngine;

  beforeEach(() => {
    engine = createTestEngine();
  });

  it("stores and retrieves a memory", async () => {
    const id = await engine.add({ content: "test", scope: "repo" });
    const memory = await engine.get(id);
    expect(memory.content).toBe("test");
  });

  it("retrieves relevant context within token budget", async () => {
    await engine.add({ content: "Use npm test before release", scope: "repo" });
    await engine.add({ content: "Database uses UUIDs", scope: "repo" });

    const pack = await engine.getContext({ task: "prepare release", budget: 500 });
    expect(pack.memoriesUsed).toBeGreaterThan(0);
    expect(pack.tokenCount).toBeLessThanOrEqual(500);
  });
});

docs.title: Testing Connectors
docs.text:
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import sampleEvent from "../fixtures/github-push.json";

describe("GitHub connector", () => {
  it("normalizes push events to memory fields", () => {
    const memories = normalizeGitHubEvent(sampleEvent);
    expect(memories[0]).toMatchObject({

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Cognibrain is a self-hosted engineering memory layer that gives coding agents durable recall across sessions. It stores corrections, repo rules, action outcomes, connector events, and patch evidence — then returns compact, relevant context before each agent action.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Modern coding agents (Codex, Cursor, Copilot, custom LLM-based tools) are stateless by default. Every session starts fresh:

  • A reviewer corrects an agent's approach → the agent makes the same mistake next time
  • A build fails for a known reason → the agent re-discovers the fix from scratch
  • Team conventions exist in scattered docs → agents miss them consistently

docs.title: How Cognibrain Solves It
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Agent starts task] --> B[Request context from Cognibrain]
    B --> C[Receive relevant memories]
    C --> D[Guard risky actions]
    D --> E[Execute work]
    E --> F[Record outcomes & corrections]
    F --> G[Memory persists for next session]
    G --> B

Cognibrain acts as a feedback loop between agent sessions:

  1. Before acting — the agent requests a context pack (corrections, conventions, past outcomes relevant to the current task)
  2. Before risky operations — the action guard warns or blocks known-bad patterns
  3. After completing work — the agent records what happened (patch evidence, corrections, new facts)
  4. Between sessions — dream cycles consolidate, deduplicate, and surface stale memories for operator review

docs.title: Integration Surfaces
docs.text:
Cognibrain exposes four surfaces, each optimized for a different consumer:

Surface Best for Protocol CLI Operators, CI/CD, shell scripts Text + JSON stdout Harness CLI Any shell-capable agent or git hook JSON stdin/stdout MCP MCP-native agents (Codex, Cursor) Model Context Protocol SDK/HTTP Product integrations and custom runtimes REST API / TypeScript / Python

All surfaces share the same underlying memory engine and can run against the same local daemon.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text: Concept Meaning Memory A durable, scoped fact that can be recalled before an agent acts Operator The human responsible for inspecting and maintaining memory state Connector An integration source/sink that ingests external events or writes back context Harness An agent lifecycle integration that calls Cognibrain for context, guards, and outcomes Dream Cycle A maintenance pass that detects stale memories and schedules operator review Action Guard A pre-action check that warns or blocks known-bad operations Patch Evidence A record of files changed, commands run, and memories used during a task

docs.title: V1 Product Shape
docs.text:
Cognibrain V1 is harness-native and CLI-backed:

  • Agent-facing moments happen through harness context, guards, warnings, outcomes, and patch evidence
  • Developer-facing inspection, repair, audit, export, and proof happen through the text-first CLI
  • There is no Operator UI or dashboard in V1 product scope

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Get Cognibrain running and store your first memory in under 5 minutes.

docs.title: 1. Install and Initialize
docs.text:
npm i @cognilabz/cognibrain
npx cognibrain init --yes

You should see output confirming the solo-dev profile is active with local storage.

docs.title: 2. Check Status
docs.text:
npx cognibrain status

This shows runtime state, memory health, active connections, and suggested next actions.

docs.title: 3. Add Your First Memory
docs.text:
npx cognibrain memories add "This repo uses npm test before every release."

Memories are durable facts that agents can recall. They persist across sessions and restarts.

docs.title: 4. Retrieve Context for a Task
docs.text:
npx cognibrain memories coding-context "prepare the release patch"

Cognibrain returns a compact context pack with relevant memories for the given task — your release memory will appear here.

docs.title: 5. Guard an Action
docs.text:
npx cognibrain guard --action "edit src/api/server.ts" --json

The action guard checks if any memories warn against or constrain the planned action. JSON output makes it easy for agents to parse programmatically.

docs.title: 6. Record Patch Evidence
docs.text:
npx cognibrain patch-evidence --task "release patch" --json

After completing work, record what files changed, what commands ran, and what memories were relevant. This builds the audit trail.

docs.title: 7. Run Proof
docs.text:
npx cognibrain proof

The proof command summarizes the current evidence state — what's been recorded, what's verified, and what needs attention.

docs.title: Full Lifecycle Example
docs.text:
Here's a complete agent lifecycle in one flow:

# Before starting work
npx cognibrain context --task "fix auth token refresh" --json

# Before a risky operation
npx cognibrain guard --action "npm test" --json

# After the operation completes
npx cognibrain outcome --command "npm test" --exit-code 0 --json

# After completing the task
npx cognibrain patch-evidence --task "fix auth token refresh" --json

# End the session
npx cognibrain session-end --json

MCP-native agents

If your agent supports MCP (Model Context Protocol), you can use the MCP integration instead of CLI commands. See MCP Integration for setup.

npx cognibrain init --benchmark --yes        # Proof lab
Flag Effect --yes Accept all defaults without prompting --profile <name> Use a specific profile (solo-dev, benchmark) --no-start Don't start the daemon after init --no-skill Skip Codex skill installation --no-doctor Skip the doctor check

JSON mode for scripting

Backward compatibility

Daemon vs local-direct

docs.title: Dream Cycles
docs.text: Dream cycles are automated memory maintenance passes that keep your memory store healthy, relevant, and contradiction-free.

docs.title: What Is a Dream Cycle?
docs.text:
A dream cycle is a periodic background process that:

  • Detects stale memories that haven't been recalled in a long time
  • Identifies contradictions between memories
  • Produces summaries by consolidating related memories
  • Schedules operator review for items that need human judgment

Think of it as garbage collection for engineering knowledge — it runs quietly and surfaces only what needs attention.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
graph TB
    A[Trigger Dream Cycle] --> B[Scan Memory Store]
    B --> C{Stale?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Flag for Review]
    C -->|No| E{Contradicts another?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Surface Contradiction]
    E -->|No| G{Related group?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Propose Summary]
    G -->|No| I[No action]
    D --> J[Operator Review Queue]
    F --> J
    H --> J

docs.title: Automatic (on session end)
docs.text:
npx cognibrain session-end --run-dream-if-due --json

This triggers a dream cycle only if enough time has passed since the last one.

docs.title: Manual
docs.text:
npx cognibrain dream-plan --json

View what the dream cycle would do without executing changes.

docs.title: From the Lifecycle
docs.text:
Dream cycles can be configured to run:

  • After every N sessions
  • On a time schedule (daily, weekly)
  • On-demand via the CLI

docs.title: Operator Review
docs.text:
When a dream cycle surfaces items for review, operators can inspect and act:

npx cognibrain memories list --status review
npx cognibrain memories approve <id>
npx cognibrain memories archive <id>

Harnesses may surface urgent review context inline, while the CLI remains the V1 surface for explicit inspection and repair.

docs.title: Staleness Detection
docs.text:
A memory becomes a staleness candidate when:

  1. It hasn't been recalled in any context pack for a configurable period
  2. It hasn't been manually referenced or updated
  3. Related memories have superseded its content

Staleness ≠ deletion

Stale memories are flagged for review, not automatically deleted. Only an operator can archive a memory.

docs.title: Contradiction Detection
docs.text:
Contradictions are detected when:

  • Two memories make opposing claims about the same topic
  • A newer correction invalidates an older fact
  • Connector events conflict with stored conventions
npx cognibrain conflicts --json

docs.title: Summary Consolidation
docs.text:
When multiple memories cover overlapping ground, the dream cycle may propose consolidating them into a single, cleaner memory. Example:

Before: - "Run npm test before release" - "Always test before publishing" - "The release script requires passing tests"

After (proposed): - "Release requires npm test to pass — enforced by the release script and CI"

Consolidation proposals require operator approval before taking effect.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Dream cycle behavior is configurable through environment variables and runtime settings:

Setting Default Description Staleness threshold 30 days Days without recall before flagging Auto-run frequency Per 10 sessions Sessions between automatic runs Max items per cycle 20 Limit on items surfaced per run

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Run regularly

Don't let memory stores grow unchecked. Regular dream cycles keep context packs fast and relevant.

Review promptly

Stale items in the review queue add noise. Approve or archive them within a few days.

Trust the consolidation

Summary proposals are conservative. If a consolidation looks right, approve it — fewer, better memories beat many overlapping ones.

docs.title: Harness Lifecycle
docs.text:
The harness lifecycle is a JSON-first shell integration that any agent, git hook, or CI runner can call. It provides the same memory capabilities as MCP but through standard shell commands.

Use MCP for MCP-native agents. Use the cognibrain harness or top-level lifecycle CLI for shell-capable agents, git hooks, and CI. Use SDK/HTTP for product integrations and custom runtimes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The harness defines a simple lifecycle loop:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant Cognibrain
    participant External as External Systems

    Agent->>Cognibrain: context (what do I need to know?)
    Cognibrain-->>Agent: context pack + relevant memories
    Agent->>Cognibrain: guard (is this action safe?)
    Cognibrain-->>Agent: allowed/warned/blocked
    Agent->>External: execute work
    External-->>Agent: result
    Agent->>Cognibrain: outcome (what happened?)
    Agent->>Cognibrain: patch-evidence (what changed?)
    Agent->>Cognibrain: session-end (done)

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: All harness commands support --json for structured output. The top-level commands are preferred for new integrations:

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Request memories relevant to the current task:

npx cognibrain context --task "prepare the release patch" --json
npx cognibrain context --task "fix auth" --repo cognilabz/cognibrain --json

docs.title: Guard
docs.text:
Check an action before executing:

npx cognibrain guard --action "npm test" --json
npx cognibrain guard --action "rm -rf node_modules" --json

Response includes allowed, warnings, and blockers.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
Record the result of a command:

npx cognibrain outcome --command "npm test" --exit-code 0 --json
npx cognibrain outcome --command "npm run build" --exit-code 1 --stderr "..." --json

docs.title: Correction
docs.text:
Store a human correction for future recall:

npx cognibrain correction --text "Use npm test, not pnpm." --json

docs.title: Patch Evidence
docs.text:
Record what files changed and what commands ran:

npx cognibrain patch-evidence \
  --task "package cleanup" \
  --files package.json \
  --commands "npm test" \
  --json

docs.title: Session End
docs.text:
Signal the end of an agent session:

npx cognibrain session-end --json
npx cognibrain session-end --run-dream-if-due --json

docs.title: Additional Commands
docs.text:
npx cognibrain release-prepare --repo cognilabz/cognibrain --json
npx cognibrain dream-plan --json
npx cognibrain source-revalidate --user local --json
npx cognibrain conflicts --json
npx cognibrain health --json

docs.title: Backward Compatibility
docs.text:
The cognibrain harness prefix is a backward-compatible alias:

# These are equivalent:
npx cognibrain context --task "fix auth" --json
npx cognibrain harness context --task "fix auth" --json

New scripts should use the top-level commands directly.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
For daemon-backed mode with auth:

# Environment variable (preferred)
export MEMORY_API_KEY=your-key
npx cognibrain context --task "..." --json

# Inline flag
npx cognibrain context --task "..." --api-key your-key --json

# Bearer token
npx cognibrain context --task "..." --bearer-token your-jwt --json

Supported auth sources:

Method Usage --api-key Inline API key --bearer-token JWT/OIDC bearer token --auth-env Read token from a named env var MEMORY_API_KEY Default API key env var COGNIBRAIN_API_KEY Alternative API key env var COGNIBRAIN_API_TOKEN Alternative token env var MEMORY_BEARER_TOKEN Bearer token env var

Production mode

In production/security mode, the harness CLI requires the daemon unless --local-direct is explicitly requested. This prevents accidental unauthenticated local access.

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
steps:
  - name: Get context
    run: npx cognibrain context --task "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" --json

  - name: Run tests
    run: npm test

  - name: Record outcome
    run: npx cognibrain outcome --command "npm test" --exit-code $? --json

docs.title: Git Hooks
docs.text:
#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/pre-push
npx cognibrain guard --action "git push" --json | jq -e '.allowed' || exit 1

docs.title: Local-Direct Mode
docs.text:
For debugging or environments without a running daemon:

npx cognibrain context --task "..." --local-direct --json

This bypasses the HTTP daemon and operates directly against local storage. Not recommended for production.

docs.title: MCP Integration
docs.text: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration lets MCP-native agents (Codex, Cursor, and others) communicate with Cognibrain directly through the standardized MCP tool interface.

docs.title: When to Use MCP
docs.text:
Use MCP when your agent host natively supports the Model Context Protocol. For agents that can only run shell commands, use the Harness Lifecycle instead.

Agent Host Recommended Surface OpenAI Codex MCP Cursor MCP Custom MCP host MCP CI/CD pipelines Harness CLI Git hooks Harness CLI Non-MCP agents Harness CLI or SDK

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
The init command automatically generates Cursor MCP configuration:

npx cognibrain init --yes
# Creates .cursor/mcp.json and .cursor/rules/open-memory.mdc

To regenerate:

npx cognibrain config cursor
Generated .cursor/mcp.json 
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cognibrain": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["cognibrain", "mcp", "serve"],
      "env": {}
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
npx cognibrain config codex
# Updates $CODEX_HOME/config.toml and writes AGENTS.md

docs.title: Manual MCP Server Start
docs.text:
For custom MCP hosts, start the MCP server directly:

npx cognibrain mcp serve

This starts an MCP stdio server that any MCP-compatible client can connect to.

docs.title: Available MCP Tools
docs.text: The MCP server exposes these tool classes:

docs.title: Context Pack
docs.text:
Retrieve compact memory context for a task before the agent begins work.

Tool: cognibrain_context
Input: { "task": "prepare the release patch", "tokenBudget": 1200 }
Output: { "context": "...", "memoriesUsed": 5 }

docs.title: Coding Context
docs.text:
Retrieve codebase-specific corrections and conventions relevant to files being edited.

Tool: cognibrain_coding_context
Input: { "task": "fix auth refresh", "files": ["src/auth.ts"] }
Output: { "corrections": [...], "conventions": [...] }

docs.title: Action Guard
docs.text:
Check a planned action against known guards before executing.

Tool: cognibrain_guard
Input: { "action": "edit src/api/server.ts" }
Output: { "allowed": true, "warnings": [] }

docs.title: Memory Add
docs.text:
Store a durable correction, decision, or fact.

Tool: cognibrain_memory_add
Input: { "content": "Use JWT RS256 for auth tokens", "scope": "repo" }
Output: { "id": "mem_abc123", "stored": true }

docs.title: Patch Evidence
docs.text:
Record files changed, commands run, and memories used during a task.

Tool: cognibrain_patch_evidence
Input: { "task": "auth fix", "files": ["src/auth.ts"], "commands": ["npm test"] }
Output: { "evidenceId": "ev_xyz789" }

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
Inspect health and trigger dream-cycle maintenance.

Tool: cognibrain_health
Input: {}
Output: { "status": "healthy", "memoryCount": 42, "staleCandidates": 2 }

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
For local development with solo-dev profile, no authentication is needed.

For daemon-backed deployments with auth enabled:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cognibrain": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["cognibrain", "mcp", "serve"],
      "env": {
        "MEMORY_API_KEY": "${env:MEMORY_API_KEY}"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: MCP vs CLI Lifecycle
docs.text:
Both MCP and CLI lifecycle commands hit the same memory engine:

graph TB
    subgraph "MCP Path"
        Agent1[MCP Agent] --> MCPServer[MCP Server]
    end

    subgraph "CLI Path"
        Agent2[Shell Agent] --> CLI[Harness CLI]
    end

    MCPServer --> Core[Memory Core]
    CLI --> Core
    Core --> Store[(Storage)]

Choose based on what your agent host supports. The memory behavior is identical regardless of surface.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
MCP server not responding

Ensure the Cognibrain daemon is running: 

npx cognibrain status
npx cognibrain start  # if stopped

Authentication errors

If you see auth errors in MCP, verify your API key: 

npx cognibrain doctor --fix

docs.title: Memory Management
docs.text: Memories are the core primitive of Cognibrain — durable, scoped facts that coding agents can recall before acting.

docs.title: What Is a Memory?
docs.text:
A memory is any piece of engineering knowledge worth preserving across sessions:

  • Corrections: "Use npm test, not pnpm test"
  • Conventions: "All API routes require auth middleware"
  • Procedures: "Run npm run build before releasing"
  • Preferences: "Use single quotes in TypeScript"
  • Evidence: "The auth refactor was completed on 2026-06-01"
  • Facts: "The database schema uses UUID primary keys"

docs.title: From the CLI
docs.text:
npx cognibrain memories add "This repo uses npm test before release."
npx cognibrain memories add "Never edit generated files in dist/" --scope repo

docs.title: From Agent Corrections
docs.text:
When an operator corrects an agent:

npx cognibrain correction --text "Use npm test, not pnpm." --json

docs.title: From Connector Events
docs.text: Connectors can automatically create memories from external events (e.g., a merged PR that changes conventions).

docs.title: Memory Scopes
docs.text:
Memories are scoped to control where they're recalled:

Scope Recalled when repo Working in the associated repository user Working as the associated user (any repo) global Always available task Relevant to specific task types 
npx cognibrain memories add "Deploy requires VPN" --scope repo
npx cognibrain memories add "I prefer verbose error messages" --scope user

docs.title: Context Pack
docs.text:
Get a curated set of memories for a specific task:

npx cognibrain context --task "fix the auth token refresh" --json

The context pack uses relevance scoring to return the most useful memories within a token budget.

docs.title: Coding Context
docs.text:
Get corrections and conventions for specific files:

npx cognibrain memories coding-context "refactor the API layer" --json

docs.title: List All
docs.text:
npx cognibrain memories list
npx cognibrain memories list --scope repo --limit 50 --json

docs.title: Memory Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active: Created
    Active --> Active: Recalled / Reinforced
    Active --> Stale: Not recalled for N days
    Stale --> Active: Recalled again
    Stale --> Review: Dream cycle flags
    Review --> Active: Operator confirms
    Review --> Archived: Operator removes
    Archived --> [*]

Memories follow a natural lifecycle:

  1. Active — recently created or recalled, participates in context packs
  2. Stale — not recalled for an extended period, candidate for review
  3. Under Review — flagged by a dream cycle for operator attention
  4. Archived — removed by operator, no longer recalled

docs.title: Token Budgets
docs.text:
When requesting context, you can control how much memory is returned:

npx cognibrain context --task "release prep" --budget 800 --json

Cognibrain ranks memories by relevance and fills the budget with the most useful items. This prevents context windows from being overwhelmed with low-value recall.

docs.title: Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
When memories contradict each other, Cognibrain uses:

  1. Recency — newer memories take precedence
  2. Source authority — operator corrections outrank auto-ingested facts
  3. Scope specificity — repo-scoped memories outrank global for in-repo work
  4. Dream cycle resolution — contradictions are surfaced for operator review
npx cognibrain conflicts --json

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Be specific

"Use npm test" is better than "Run tests". Specific memories are easier to match and recall.

Include context

"In the auth module, always validate JWT expiry before refresh" beats "Validate JWT expiry".

Let agents self-correct

Configure your agent to call cognibrain correction whenever it receives human feedback. This builds memory organically.

Don't store secrets

Never store API keys, tokens, or passwords as memories. Use environment variables and reference them by name.

docs.title: Docker Deployment
docs.text:
Cognibrain provides optional Docker packaging for containerized deployments. Docker is not required — it's an alternative to native service installation.

Docker is optional. The CLI is the required control plane for setup, status, verification, and service management; Docker only packages the same runtime for container platforms.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Build
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile -t cognibrain:latest .

# Run
docker run -d \
  --name cognibrain \
  -p 8787:8787 \
  -e MEMORY_API_KEY=your-key \
  -e MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL=postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/cognibrain \
  -v cognibrain-data:/app/.cognibrain \
  cognibrain:latest

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
version: "3.9"

services:
  cognibrain:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: docker/Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "8787:8787"
    environment:
      MEMORY_API_KEY: ${MEMORY_API_KEY}
      MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL: postgresql://cognibrain:secret@postgres:5432/cognibrain
      MEMORY_POLICY_MODE: production
    volumes:
      - cognibrain-data:/app/.cognibrain
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: cognibrain
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: cognibrain
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U cognibrain"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  cognibrain-data:
  postgres-data:

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: Deployment manifests are provided under deploy/:

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cognibrain
  labels:
    app: cognibrain
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cognibrain
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cognibrain
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: cognibrain
          image: cognibrain:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8787
          env:
            - name: MEMORY_API_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: cognibrain-secrets
                  key: api-key
            - name: MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: cognibrain-secrets
                  key: postgres-url
            - name: MEMORY_POLICY_MODE
              value: "production"
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /api/health
              port: 8787
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 30
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /api/health
              port: 8787
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "256Mi"
              cpu: "250m"
            limits:
              memory: "512Mi"
              cpu: "500m"

docs.text:
All configuration environment variables work in Docker. Key ones for container deployments:

Variable Required Description MEMORY_API_KEY Yes API authentication MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL Recommended Database connection MEMORY_POLICY_MODE Recommended Set to production COGNIBRAIN_HOST No Bind to 0.0.0.0 for container access COGNIBRAIN_PORT No Default 8787

docs.title: Monitoring & Health
docs.text: Keep your Cognibrain deployment healthy with built-in health checks, observability hooks, and operational runbooks.

docs.title: CLI Health
docs.text:
cognibrain status          # Human-readable overview
cognibrain health --json   # Machine-readable health
cognibrain doctor --fix    # Diagnose and repair

docs.title: HTTP Health Endpoint
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:8787/api/health

{
  "status": "healthy",
  "memoryCount": 42,
  "staleCandidates": 2,
  "uptime": 86400,
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "storage": "postgres",
  "lastDreamCycle": "2026-06-10T08:00:00Z"
}

Use this endpoint for:

  • Container liveness/readiness probes
  • Load balancer health checks
  • Monitoring system polling

docs.title: Connector Health
docs.text:
cognibrain connections doctor

Checks all configured connectors for reachability and valid credentials.

docs.title: Operational Runbook
docs.text:
Daily/weekly operator checklist:

# 1. Check overall health
cognibrain status

# 2. Fix any detected issues
cognibrain doctor --fix

# 3. Review memory state
cognibrain proof

# 4. Check for stale memories needing review
cognibrain memories list --status review

# 5. Verify connectors
cognibrain connections doctor

# 6. Run release checks (if maintaining the package)
npm run release:check

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text:
Monitor these indicators for a healthy deployment:

Metric Healthy Range Action if Unhealthy Memory count Growing steadily Check if agents are recording Stale candidates < 10% of total Run dream cycle, review items Last dream cycle < 7 days ago Trigger manually or check schedule Response time (p95) < 200ms Check storage backend, indexing Error rate < 1% Check logs for patterns Storage usage Below capacity Archive old memories, verify cleanup

docs.title: Health Check Failure
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# alert-on-unhealthy.sh
STATUS=$(curl -s http://localhost:8787/api/health | jq -r '.status')
if [ "$STATUS" != "healthy" ]; then
  echo "ALERT: Cognibrain unhealthy — status: $STATUS"
  # Send to your alerting system
fi

docs.title: Service Down
docs.text:
Monitor the service manager:

# systemd
systemctl is-active cognibrain.service

# Or check the PID
cognibrain service status

docs.title: Service Logs
docs.text:
cognibrain service logs           # Recent logs
journalctl -u cognibrain --since "1 hour ago"  # systemd

docs.title: Log Levels
docs.text:
Set via environment:

export COGNIBRAIN_LOG_LEVEL=debug  # debug, info, warn, error
cognibrain service restart

docs.title: Dream Cycle Monitoring
docs.text:
Dream cycles should run regularly. Monitor:

# Check last run
cognibrain health --json | jq '.lastDreamCycle'

# Manual trigger if overdue
cognibrain dream-plan --json

npm run internal -- verify:postgres

# Check connection count
psql "$MEMORY_POSTGRES_URL" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'cognibrain';"
